digest.top_line: Ohri liver SBRT pooled analysis: mets 3y LC 93% vs 65% at BED >100 vs ≤100 Gy10 (P<.001); HCC/CCA primaries show no BED effect (P=.972).
digest.tldr: Liver mets carry the day's actionable RT signal: BED >100 Gy10 tracks with 3y LC 93% vs 65%, while HCC/CCA primaries show no dose effect. BED is confounded with institution across 13 pooled series. ReTEC cord reirradiation modeling implies faster recovery than Nelson 2009, but the 1-yr CI is 31%-95%; authors advise staying within current guidelines.

sites.intro: HyTEC methods primer: a two-parameter logistic fit needs ≥20 events, and median-split screens give different answers depending on the test chosen.

studies.name: A Primer on Dose-Response Data Modeling in Radiation Therapy
studies.tldr: HyTEC lung example: 13/96 grade 2+ RP; logistic MLE fit beat the null by LL 6.66 (p=0.0003); single cut-points imply dependence that may not exist.
details: 🔍 Methods review from the HyTEC effort; worked example pools 2 published lung datasets, grade 2+ RP vs MLD
📊 13/96 events (13.5%); median MLD 3.05 Gy
📐 Rule of thumb cited: ≥10 events per model parameter, ≥20 for a two-parameter logistic fit

details.text: 🔍 Four-step workflow and the method used for each
⚠️ Median-split screen depends on which test is picked
subdetails: Wilcoxon rank sum p=0.002 when assumptions go unchecked

details: 📊 Setting 10% toxicity as acceptable gives MLD 3.27 Gy; NPV for MLD<3.27 Gy 52/56 = 92.9%
⚠️ D50 and γ50 are correlated ('banana' iso-LL); a CI rectangle from the two separate CIs is wrong
⚠️ Low-event (spinal cord) or high-control (prostate TCP) data sit far from D50; predictions hinge on small γ50 shifts
⚠️ No volume effect modeled: pooled literature lacks full DVH, so MLD cannot be converted to mean EQD2
studies.significance: The tails of a dose-response curve, where serial-organ constraints and escalation arguments live, are the least data-constrained: with very low or very high event rates, predicted risk swings with small γ50 shifts. Read a HyTEC constraint by its NPV and data range, not the fit p-value, and treat extrapolation past the treated dose range as unvalidated.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Methods review from the **HyTEC** effort. Worked example pools two published datasets, **grade 2+ radiation pneumonitis vs mean lung dose**, fit with a logistic model by maximum likelihood using in-house code cross-validated by HyTEC contributors.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **13/96 events (13.5%)**, median MLD 3.05 Gy. The likelihood ratio test rejected the no-relationship null (**difference 6.66, p=0.0003**). At a 10% acceptable toxicity level (MLD 3.27 Gy), **NPV was 52/56 = 92.9%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Same fitting approach underlies the HyTEC site papers that used **mean dose for liver** and **maximum dose for optic pathways**. Spinal cord NTCP and prostate TCP from HyTEC illustrate the extreme parameter correlation seen when data cluster at low or high response.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: 13 events is **below the 20-event floor** the authors cite for a two-parameter model. Volume effect (LKB, relative seriality) is not modeled because pooled data rarely carry full DVH, and machine-learning approaches are set aside.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Dose-volume metrics are at best **surrogates** for an aggregate of drivers, so statistical significance does not establish dependence. A single cut-point carries a **fixed risk tolerance** that may be too strict or too loose for a given pt.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this piece for a practicing radiation oncologist is less the logistic fit itself than the audit trail it lays out behind every constraint pulled from a HyTEC table. Each published threshold rests on three separable steps: a parameter fit, a test that the fit beats a flat line, and an uncertainty band on the predicted risk. The authors' point is that error in one step carries into the next, so a constraint reported without all three is one whose reliability the reader cannot judge.

The worked lung example is useful because it is borderline. 13 events in 96 pts falls under the 20-event floor the authors themselves cite for a two-parameter model, and the median-split screen is fragile: whether the signal looks real depends on which test was run, from a Fisher exact p of 0.070 to an inappropriate rank-sum p of 0.002. The likelihood ratio test does clear the null (p=0.0003), but the same dataset can read as marginal or emphatic depending on choices made before any curve is drawn. That should make a reader wary of how many published dose-response signals reflect analytic flexibility rather than biology.

The correlated-parameter section is the one most clinicians skip and the one with the most practical weight. When event rates are very low, as with myelitis, or very high, as with prostate tumor control, the data sit far from the 50% point where the slope is defined, so small shifts in γ50 move predicted risk at the doses we actually prescribe. The tails of the curve, exactly where serial-organ constraints are set and where escalation is argued, are the least constrained by data. Carrying a curve built on modest-dose cohorts into a hypofractionated regimen that pushes higher is the scenario where model shape and parameter interplay matter most, and where the bootstrap bands widen.

The NPV framing shifts how a constraint should be read in clinic. A threshold earns trust by how often pts who meet it avoid toxicity, not by the p-value of the fit. The authors also argue that a single cut-point treated as universal bakes in a risk tolerance (their examples are symptomatic pneumonitis and myelitis budgets) that may be wrong for a given pt in either direction, whether accepting more risk to push tumor control or less in someone for whom the toxicity could be fatal.

What the paper does not settle is how often published constraints would fail these checks. Its single lung example cannot answer that. Volume effect is absent because pooled literature rarely supplies full DVH, which also blocks EQD2 harmonization of mean dose across fractionation schemes, and the authors explicitly decline to call these methods preferred. It is a guide to reading a model critically, not a validated recipe, and its strongest practical message is to look at the raw data, the data range, and the confidence band before trusting the curve.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The tails of a dose-response curve, where serial-organ constraints and escalation arguments live, are the least data-constrained: with very low or very high event rates, predicted risk swings with small γ50 shifts. Read a HyTEC constraint by its NPV and data range, not the fit p-value, and treat extrapolation past the treated dose range as unvalidated.

open_questions: Volume-effect models once pooled full-DVH datasets are accessible
Mean-dose EQD2 harmonization across fractionation without full DVH
How often published NTCP constraints fail significance and CI checks

sites.intro: The pooled ReTEC model favors faster cord recovery than Nelson 2009, but the uncertainty is too wide to loosen reirradiation limits.

studies.name: ReTEC spinal cord reirradiation NTCP
studies.tldr: Pooled 282 lesions (six myelopathies): cord recovery >50% in <1 yr, but 1-yr CI 31%-95%; authors advise staying within current reirradiation guidelines.
details: 📊 NTCP model from 13 papers, 282 lesions, six myelopathy cases
📊 ML fit: tRH 4 mo, Rmax 95% (p<0.01, LRT); recovery >50% in <1 yr
📐 Recovery at a 1-yr interval: bootstrap 95% CI 31%-95%

details.text: 📊 Reference case (cord Dmax 50 Gy/25 fx, then 15.5 Gy/5 fx at 1 yr) by recovery scenario
⚠️ Recovery factor and refitted NTCP curve only hold as a matched set
subdetails: No-recovery dose (140 Gy) on ML curve: 27% risk
ML dose (60 Gy) on no-recovery curve: <0.001% risk

details: 🔍 Inclusion: per-pt prior and reirradiation cord Dmax, interval, fractionation or BED, ≥1 SBRT course
🔍 Clinical demo with 33% recovery: composite 5-fx equivalent cord Dmax 28 Gy vs TG-101 30 Gy/5 fx
🔗 vs Nelson 2009: ML recovery faster and more complete than the 33% at 1 yr in clinical use
⚠️ Dmax-only inputs; no voxel-wise composite reirradiation plans found in the literature

verdict.rationale: Proof-of-concept fit anchored on six myelopathy events and Dmax-only data; recovery CI 31%-95%. Authors themselves advise against acting on it.
verdict.audience: Spine reirradiation with SBRT, prior cord dose within tolerance, ≥5 mo interval

studies.significance: The recovery factor and the NTCP curve refitted after it work only as a pair. Mixing them gives 27% or <0.001% risk, while each matched set puts the reference case under 1%. So a recovery discount loaded into planning software has to carry its own dose-response fit, and the interval decision still rests on HyTEC and Nelson limits.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with spine mets needing SBRT reirradiation after a first course within cord tolerance and ≥5 months earlier, this supports planning to existing HyTEC/Nelson cord limits; it does not extend to a first course that exceeded tolerance or to a shorter interval.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Pooled analysis of published reirradiation series: **13 papers, 282 lesions, six myelopathy cases**. Recovery factors (raised-exponential model with tRH and Rmax) and logistic NTCP parameters fitted by **maximum likelihood**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Required per-pt or homogeneous-group reporting of **prior and reirradiation cord Dmax, interval between courses, and fractionation or BED**, with **≥1 SBRT course** and myelopathy outcome in the absence of progression. Cord proper and cauda equina pooled; brainstem and sacral plexus excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: All doses converted to **BED2 (α/β = 2 Gy)**. Reference case: **50 Gy/25 fx (BED2 100 Gy)** followed by **15.5 Gy/5 fx (BED2 40 Gy)** to the same level after 1 yr.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Radiation myelopathy in the absence of progression. Modeled outputs: cord recovery fraction over time and NTCP vs time-discounted composite BED2.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Recovery is faster and fuller than the **Nelson 2009 33% at 1 yr** assumption in current use. Under Nelson's values the **HyTEC** cord tables are mutually compatible at **12 months or more**; the ML model gives compatibility at **5-6 months**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents spinal cord or cauda reirradiation with at least one SBRT course, a prior cord dose within tolerance, and an interval of at least 5 months. Does not represent a first course that exceeded tolerance, conventional-only reirradiation, brainstem, or sacral plexus.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The Rmax search was **capped at 95%** and the fit reached the cap. Non-SBRT data suggested slower recovery and were excluded with no definite reason identified. Fewer than half of pts with mets treated with spine SBRT may be alive at 1 yr, against a **6-month median latency** after reirradiation, so late events are likely missed.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The model is only valid as a full parameter set applied in the order it was built, not as a standalone recovery percentage. Authors recommend **staying within current guidelines** until voxel-wise composite datasets, the stated ReTEC goal, confirm or refute these estimates.

studies.interpretation:
The question this paper takes on is how much prior cord dose can be discounted before an SBRT reirradiation, and its honest answer is that the published record cannot yet say. Current practice relies on the Nelson 2009 assumption of 33% recovery at a year and on the HyTEC reirradiation table, which allows a cord Dmax of 15.5 Gy in 5 fractions after a 50 Gy in 25 fraction first course. The maximum likelihood fit here points to much faster and fuller recovery (tRH 4 months, Rmax 95%), but the bootstrap interval at a 1-year gap runs from 31% to 95%. The lower bound sits close to the Nelson figure. So the data do not rule out the conservative assumption already in use. What they fail to rule out is something far more permissive.

The more durable contribution is structural. A recovery factor and the dose-response curve refitted after it are one object. Refit the curve under any of the three recovery assumptions and the reference case lands under 1% risk every time, because that case sits near the centroid of the pooled data. Mix the parts and the estimate swings from 27% to below 0.001%. This matters for anyone who imports a published recovery percentage into a planning system and checks the composite against a de novo constraint: the percentage means nothing without the curve it was fitted with. The workflow the authors show, converting the discounted composite to a five-fraction equivalent and checking it against the TG-101 limit of 30 Gy in 5 fractions, keeps that pairing visible.

Confidence in the recovery estimates should be low, and not only because of the event count. Six myelopathy cases across 282 lesions means very few positives anchor the curve. Every input is a point maximum. The two courses' hot spots often sit in different places, so summing Dmax values plausibly overstates the true composite in many lesions, and that bias would push the fit toward apparent recovery. Competing mortality pushes the other way. Fewer than half of pts treated with spine SBRT for metastases may be alive at a year, and median latency to myelopathy is 6 months after reirradiation, so late events are plausibly missed and risk underestimated. The fit also hit its own 95% ceiling on Rmax. Non-SBRT data, which suggested slower recovery, were set aside without an identified cause, which leaves open whether the SBRT-only result reflects biology or selection.

What would have to be true for the fast-recovery reading to hold? Voxel-wise composite dose with per-pt fractionation, consistent definitions of the interval between courses, and follow-up long enough to capture late myelopathy. That is what the ReTEC proposal, and prospective efforts such as REPAIR and ReCare, could supply. Until then the paper is best read as reassurance that the HyTEC and Nelson constraints are not obviously unsafe, compatible with each other at intervals of 12 months or more under Nelson's assumptions. It is not permission to shorten intervals toward the 5-6 months at which the ML model shows compatibility, and the authors say as much.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The ML fit has the HyTEC cord limits holding at 5-6 month intervals, against 12 months or more under Nelson's 33% recovery, but the 1-yr recovery CI spans 31%-95%. The interval and cord Dmax decision stays anchored to existing guidelines, and any recovery discount used in planning must stay paired with its own NTCP curve.

open_questions: Validation with voxel-wise composite reirradiation plans
Cord recovery when no course used SBRT

sites.intro: In pooled, reconstructed lesion-level data, BED >100 Gy10 matters for liver mets but not for HCC/CCA primaries.

studies.name: Local Control After SBRT for Liver Tumors (Ohri)
studies.tldr: Liver mets: 3y LC 93% vs 65% at BED >100 vs ≤100 Gy10 (P<.001); primaries show no BED effect (P=.972), 3y LC 86%.

details.text: 📊 Actuarial LC by tumor type (log-rank P=.011, primary vs mets)
📊 Actuarial LC by BED within tumor type
📐 TCP model, liver mets: modeled 2y LC by BED (bootstrap 95% CI), R2 0.98

details: 🔍 Pooled lesion-level analysis of 13 published series: 721 tumors (642 pts), 79 local failures
🔍 Lesion data reconstructed from published KM curves (Guyot method); wide-BED series excluded

subdetails: Liver mets: 6 studies, n=290; CRC 56% of mets

details: 🔍 Doses 24-60 Gy in 1-5 fx of 7-26 Gy; median BED 88 Gy10 (IQR 72-125), α/β=10
📊 Primaries: 227 lesions at BED 60-72 Gy10 reached 2y LC 90%
⚠️ BED compared across series, so dose is confounded with institution, histology and case mix
⚠️ Tumor size unavailable; Yamashita et al found LC 64% vs 85% for >30 vs ≤30 mm
⚠️ KM LC without competing risks; many pts die before local failure
⚠️ HCC often pretreated (TACE/lipiodol), so viable burden at SBRT may be lower than mets

verdict.rationale: Pooled reconstruction of single-arm series; BED effect is a between-study comparison confounded by histology, size and institution. Design, not maturity, limits the dose-response claim.
verdict.audience: Primary (HCC, CCA) or metastatic liver tumors, SBRT in 1-5 fx

studies.significance: The TCP fit (Fig 4) makes BED 100 Gy10 a waypoint, not a ceiling: modeled 2-year LC for mets rises from 70% at 80 Gy10 (10 Gy × 4) to 76% at 100 Gy10 and 90% at 180 Gy10 (20 Gy × 3). The flat primary curve may reflect pretreated, smaller viable tumor rather than absent dose-response.
studies.monday_clinic: In a liver metastasis planned for SBRT, this supports a schedule above BED 100 Gy10 where normal-liver constraints allow; in HCC or cholangiocarcinoma with underlying liver disease, it does not support escalating past conservative 8-10 Gy × 5 schedules.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Systematic quantitative review: PubMed search Nov 16, 2013 (201 hits), **13 series** pooled. Individual lesion data were **reconstructed from published KM curves**, and series using a wide BED range without dose-level outcomes were excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **721 tumors (642 pts)**: HCC n=394, liver mets n=290 (CRC 56%), CCA n=37. Excluded SBRT as bridge to transplant, reviews, case reports and overlapping cohorts.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **24-60 Gy in 1-5 fx** of 7-26 Gy; median **BED 88 Gy10** (IQR 72-125), LQ model with α/β=10. Prescription point varied (isocenter, PTV, 65-80% IDL); the authors report adjustment did not alter results.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** local control, per lesion, actuarial, on serial CT/MRI (mostly every 3 mo) by RECIST, mRECIST, WHO or EASL. Median f/u 18 mo for primaries (IQR 11-29), 14 mo for mets (IQR 8-23).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Mets show a **BED-dependent LC gap (P<.001)**; primaries show **no dose-response (P=.972)** across BED 60-180 Gy10, including other cutoffs tested.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors place the metastatic dose-response alongside **lung SBRT and spine/other metastasis** dose-response data. For HCC, results align with a prospective trial using a wide SBRT dose range; NCT01730937 is an ongoing cooperative group study using NTCP-guided dosing.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents HCC, CCA and liver metastases (majority CRC) treated with 1-5 fx SBRT at BED 60-180 Gy10. Does not represent 90Y selective internal RT, multifocal disease, or SBRT as a bridge to transplant.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **No competing-risks analysis**, so KM LC may be biased where pts die before local failure. Post-SBRT liver imaging is hard to read, and mets follow-up is short at a median 14 mo; **no histology-specific analysis** of CRC vs other mets.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The mets signal supports **ablative BED >100 Gy10**, but its size likely includes institutional and case-mix confounding. The flat primary curve **does not show HCC lacks a dose-response**; NTCP-driven dosing and prior liver-directed therapy plausibly mask one.

studies.interpretation:
This pooled analysis is most useful because it separates two questions that liver SBRT practice tends to merge. For metastases, the data line up as a dose-response: lesions treated above BED 100 Gy10 held 3-year local control at 93% against 65% at lower doses, and a TCP fit across four BED groups tracks the observed control closely (R2 0.98). For HCC and cholangiocarcinoma, local control at BED ≤100 and >100 Gy10 is near-identical (P=.972), and the authors found the same null at other cutoffs between 60 and 180 Gy10. The same method gives opposite answers, and the method is the first thing to weigh.

Every BED comparison here is between series, not within patients. Series with wide dose ranges were excluded, so each study contributes essentially one dose level, and BED travels with institution, era, imaging protocol, prescription convention and case mix. The metastatic signal is partly a comparison of which programs chose aggressive schedules and the patients they chose them for. Tumor size, which the authors flag as the likeliest hidden driver (citing Yamashita et al, 64% vs 85% for lesions >30 vs ≤30 mm), was unavailable. If larger or colorectal lesions clustered in the lower-BED series, the gap overstates the dose effect. The direction agrees with lung and spine SBRT, which makes it plausible, but the magnitude is best read as an upper-range estimate.

The null result for primaries needs the opposite caution. HCC here was often pretreated with chemoembolization, so viable tumor at SBRT may be small, and NTCP-guided prescribing in diseased livers ties lower dose to sicker livers and plausibly to different tumors. A flat curve under those conditions does not show that HCC lacks a dose-response. It shows that, within commonly used schedules, conservative dosing achieved high control, with 227 lesions at BED 60-72 Gy10 reaching 90% 2-year control. That supports the authors' comfort with 8-10 Gy × 5 when liver function is the binding constraint. It does not argue against escalation in a well-compensated liver with a large, untreated tumor.

Two measurement issues push the same way. Kaplan-Meier local control without a competing-risks frame misstates failure risk when many patients die first, and post-SBRT liver imaging is hard to interpret, so misclassified progression can blur or distort any dose effect. Metastatic follow-up was a median of 14 months, short for late local failure after lower-dose schedules, and the analysis could not test whether colorectal histology drives the primary-versus-metastatic gap.

The metastatic conclusion would fail if a patient-level or within-study analysis showed the BED gap collapsing after adjustment for size and histology. Until that exists, the practical read is that ablative BED for liver metastases has the best pooled support available, that the modeled curve keeps rising past 100 Gy10 rather than plateauing there, and that the comparative question (SBRT against resection, thermal ablation or systemic therapy alone) remains unanswered by design, as the authors themselves state.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The TCP fit (Fig 4) makes BED 100 Gy10 a waypoint, not a ceiling: modeled 2-year LC for mets rises from 70% at 80 Gy10 to 76% at 100 Gy10 and 90% at 180 Gy10. For HCC/CCA, 227 lesions at BED 60-72 Gy10 reached 90% 2-year LC, supporting conservative dosing where liver function constrains.

open_questions: Does histology (CRC vs other) shift the liver mets TCP curve?
Is there an HCC dose-response after adjusting for tumor size?
Does liver SBRT beat other local therapies in randomized trials?

papers.title: Reirradiation treatment effects in the clinic (ReTEC) proposal – proof of concept based on spinal cord dose tolerance for reirradiation with stereotactic body radiotherapy
papers.journal: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Since the inception of spinal radiosurgery decades ago, the factors influencing spinal cord recovery have remained unclear. Elucidating these factors would aid in reirradiation planning and delivery. We describe modeling reirradiation normal tissue complication probabilities (NTCP) from compiled published data, akin to the collaborative Quantitative Analysis of Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic (QUANTEC) and High Dose per Fraction, Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic (HyTEC) projects. Purpose Simple dose‐time recovery factors for the spinal cord serve as a basis to propose the Reirradiation Treatment Effects in the Clinic (ReTEC) project. ReTEC aims to define human organ recovery factors to convert the total composite dose to an equivalent physical dose compatible with the de novo therapy dose tolerance limits. Additionally, we present a system for automating analyses as well as clinical implementation of radiation dose‐time recovery. Methods Published literature was queried for stereotactic voxel‐wise composite reirradiation plans involving the spinal cord, but none were found. Hence, minimum reporting criteria were used instead: spinal cord maximum dose (Dmax) of each course, time interval between courses, and number of fractions or biologically effective dose, per patient or in sufficiently homogeneous groups of patients. Recovery factors and logistic model parameters were fitted with maximum likelihood techniques. Results An NTCP model was derived from 13 papers with data from 282 lesions, including six myelopathy cases. The model suggested spinal cord recovery of more than 50% in less than 1 year, which is faster and more complete than current clinical practice, but with wide confidence intervals (CI) (bootstrap 95% CI: 31%–95% when the time interval was 1 year). Conclusion Due to limited data, we recommend remaining within current standard guidelines until more comprehensive analyses, optimally under the ReTEC initiative, refute or validate these estimates. ReTEC would require composite plans accounting for differing Dmax locations in each course. Nevertheless, this proof‐of‐concept Dmax model provides insight and serves as a basis to propose ReTEC.

papers.title: A Primer on Dose-Response Data Modeling in Radiation Therapy
